copies.headline: Noah's Backfield Against John's Everything Else
copies.body:
John wins this on the edges. Bowers and McBride is an obscene tight end room for a league where most teams are starting a guy who catches three balls a game, and Puka Nacua is the single highest-projected player in the matchup by a comfortable margin. Add Kyren Williams and Swift as a functional RB2 floor and there's no position where John is actually exposed. Stafford or Caleb Williams is a coin flip that lands fine either way.
Noah's path is Achane and Cook going nuclear, because the receiving room is thin fast. Garrett Wilson is legitimate, then it's Mike Evans hoping the target share holds and Michael Wilson praying Arizona throws 40 times. Colston Loveland at tight end is a rookie projection dressed up as a plan. If the running backs combine for 40, Noah steals it. If they combine for 25, this is over by the late window.

copies.headline: Isaac's Receivers Against Kaleb's Backfield
copies.body:
Two points separate these rosters on paper, and the split is clean: Isaac wins at wideout, Kaleb wins everywhere else. Ja'Marr Chase and Malik Nabers is the best top-two receiving pair in this game by a wide margin, and Isaac still has Terry McLaurin and DK Metcalf sitting behind them for flex work. The problem is everything under that. Bo Nix is a QB1 in name only next to Justin Herbert, T.J. Hockenson and Dalton Kincaid are the same nine-point coin flip, and the running back room leans on Javonte Williams and Cam Skattebo, neither of whom has a guaranteed workload.
Kaleb's edge is Ashton Jeanty and Breece Hall, which is real volume in a week where volume is the whole game. Drake London and Ladd McConkey are steady rather than explosive, and Harold Fannin Jr. quietly wins the tight end spot. Isaac needs a Chase blowup. Kaleb just needs his backs to touch the ball twenty times each.

copies.headline: Grant's Receivers Against CJ's Running Back Hoard
copies.body:
The gap here is at wideout, where Grant has an actual WR1 and CJ has a committee. Amon-Ra St. Brown is the safest floor in this matchup, Zay Flowers is Baltimore's most targeted receiver, and Jaylen Waddle and Christian Watson give Grant real WR3 choices instead of coin flips. CJ counters with Rashee Rice and Emeka Egbuka, both of whom can pop, plus Parker Washington and Alec Pierce, who are the kind of names you start in Week 1 and regret by Week 4. Tight end is a wash — Dallas Goedert versus Jake Ferguson, two guys who catch six for fifty and disappear.
CJ's edge is Joe Burrow over Kyler Murray and a backfield stuffed to the gills: Jonathan Taylor, Quinshon Judkins, Chuba Hubbard, TreVeyon Henderson. That's four startable backs and only two slots. Grant leans on Omarion Hampton's volume. Four points is nothing — one Rice touchdown flips it.

copies.headline: Logan's Philly Stack Meets Adam's Depth Problem
copies.body:
Logan's edge is the top of his roster and it's not subtle. Jalen Hurts and Saquon Barkley in the same lineup is a leverage play more than a hedge — one Philadelphia touchdown drive pays twice, and if the Eagles grind out a 27-point afternoon, Adam is chasing all day. Jeremiyah Love behind him is a real RB2, which is more than Adam can say. Adam's backfield is Kenneth Walker III in a new Kansas City role nobody has seen live yet, Bucky Irving, and Rico Dowdle — three guys who could each go for 18 or 6 with equal plausibility.
Adam wins receiver, barely, on Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Chris Olave, and he owns the tight end spot outright with LaPorta and Andrews on the bench. But Logan's wideout room is seven deep and Adam's fourth-best is Jalen Coker. The eight-point gap is real. Adam needs Walker to be the guy immediately.

copies.headline: Two Points Apart, One Tight End Problem
copies.body:
Christian's edge is his receiving corps and it's real: CeeDee Lamb and DeVonta Smith are as safe a top-two as anyone rolls out Week 1, with Jameson Williams and Khalil Shakir behind them as legitimate flex answers. The backfield is deep without a true anchor — Chase Brown and Travis Etienne carry it, Bhayshul Tuten and Aaron Jones are lottery tickets. The problem is tight end, where George Kittle is projected at zero and Chig Okonkwo is the fallback. That's a four-point hole against Tucker Kraft before anyone touches the field.
Peter counters with the two best individual pieces in the game: Lamar Jackson and Bijan Robinson, both capable of turning a two-point projection gap into a blowout by themselves. His receiver room is flatter — George Pickens, A.J. Brown and Tee Higgins all cluster around 13-14 with no separation. Christian wins if the middle of his roster shows up. Peter wins if his stars just do their jobs.

copies.headline: Mitchell's Depth Chart Beats Leif's Nameplates
copies.body:
Leif's roster reads like a 2022 draft board, and that's not entirely a compliment. Josh Allen and Christian McCaffrey are still the two safest bets in this game, and Derrick Henry behind them means the top end holds up fine. It's the middle that worries. Davante Adams, Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jayden Reed is a receiving corps built on hope more than volume, Kyle Pitts remains the league's longest-running unfinished project, and Patrick Mahomes rotting on the bench is roughly eight points of nothing.
Mitchell wins this by having four usable options everywhere. Jahmyr Gibbs and Josh Jacobs is a cleaner one-two than it looks on paper, Nico Collins is the best pure target-earner in the matchup, and Courtland Sutton, DJ Moore and Matthew Golden give him three coin flips instead of one. Tyler Warren over Travis Kelce is the tell that he's actually reading his own roster. Six-point edge, and the safer floor too.

intro: Isaac at Kaleb is the one to watch, two of the deepest rosters on the slate separated by two projected points, which means it'll come down to whichever kicker remembers he plays football. Elsewhere, Logan and John enter as the only teams projected north of 121, while Christian and Noah are staring down the barrel at 110 and 112 and hoping projections are just a suggestion. Nothing's at stake yet except a full week of talking, which around here is worth more than the win.
